scenes.sub: Every expression has a value category. It decides what you can do with it.
scenes.say: lvalues and rvalues. Every expression in C plus plus has a category, and it decides what you can do with that expression: take its address, assign to it, or move from it.

scenes.head: The rule of thumb

panels.code:
int x = 5;            // x is an lvalue, 5 is an rvalue
int* p = &x;          // ok: x has an address
int* q = &5;          // can't take the address of 5
x + 1 = 7;            // can't assign to a temporary

int& at(int i);       // returns a reference
at(0) = 3;            // ok: at(0) is an lvalue

scenes.say: An lvalue names an object that persists, like x. It has an address, and you can assign to it. An rvalue is a temporary value, like five, or x plus one. Taking its address or assigning to it fails, and G C C says lvalue required. It's about the expression, not the type. A function returning a reference gives an lvalue, so you can assign to at of zero.

scenes.head: What references can bind to

panels.code:
int x = 5;
int& a = x;               // ok
int& b = 5;               // lvalue ref to rvalue
const int& c = 5;         // ok: temporary lives on
int&& d = 5;              // ok
int&& e = x;              // rvalue ref to lvalue
int&& g = std::move(x);   // ok: now an rvalue

scenes.say: This is why it matters. int ampersand binds only to lvalues. A const reference is the exception: it binds to anything, and extends a temporary's lifetime. int and and, an rvalue reference, binds only to rvalues. That's the trick behind move semantics: an rvalue is a temporary nobody else can see, or something you marked on purpose, so it's safe to steal from. And s t d move turns x into an rvalue, so it binds.

scenes.head: The full picture (C++11)
scenes.say: Since C plus plus eleven there are actually three categories. A gl value has identity. An rvalue is the other half: something you can move from. Where they overlap: an lvalue has identity but can't be moved from implicitly. An x value, like s t d move of x, has identity and can be moved from. And a pr value is a pure temporary, like five, with no identity.

scenes.head: Trap: a named rvalue reference is an lvalue
scenes.say: The favorite interview trap. Inside take, the parameter's type is an rvalue reference. But the expression s has a name, so it's an lvalue. Using it copies. To move from it, you have to s t d move it again. Type and value category are two different things.

lines: lvalue: has identity and a name; you can take its address.
rvalue: a temporary or something cast with std::move; safe to move from.
A named rvalue reference is itself an lvalue.
scenes.say: An lvalue has identity, you can take its address. An rvalue is a temporary, or something marked with s t d move, so it's safe to move from. And a named rvalue reference is itself an lvalue.
